bodyHtml:
Passing an evaluation gets you a funded account: an account where the firm pays you a share of the profits you make. At most futures firms this stage is still simulated. Topstep calls its Express Funded Account "the simulated funded-level account you earn after passing", and Apex calls its Performance Account a "Simulated Funded (Sim Funded) account". Payouts are real money, paid by the firm from its own funds, as PF-01 explained.

This chapter covers the rules that decide when you can be paid, how much, and what each payout does to your safety margin. All rules are quoted as of September 2026 from each firm's help pages. Check them again before relying on them.

Key takeaways

  • Funded rules differ from evaluation rules. Read them before your first funded trade, not when you want your first payout.
  • Most plans need a set number of qualifying profitable days, a minimum balance or profit, and sometimes a consistency rule before each payout.
  • At several firms the first payout moves your loss floor up. After that, the money you leave in the account is your only buffer.
  • A bigger payout means a thinner buffer. Decide in advance how much to take and how much to leave.

What changes when you are funded

The account usually starts again. Topstep and MFFU both start the funded balance at $0, with the loss floor at −$2,000 on a $50K plan: Topstep says the "50K" label "refers to your buying power, not your starting balance". Apex keeps the $50,000 balance and uses a fixed safety net. Either way, you begin with the same $2,000 of room you had in the evaluation, not with your evaluation profit.

Three new kinds of rule appear:

  • Payout eligibility: what you must do before you can ask to be paid.
  • Payout size: the minimum and maximum per request, and your share (the split).
  • What happens after a payout: changes to the floor, the day count, or the number of payouts left.

Payout eligibility, $50K plans

Topstep XFA, Standard path

Qualifying days: 5 winning days of $150+

Other conditions: none beyond the days

Amount per request: 50% of balance, cap $2,000

Your split: 90%

Apex EOD Performance Account

Qualifying days: 5 days of $250+

Other conditions: balance of $52,600 to request; 50% consistency

Amount per request: $500 minimum; caps rise from $1,500 to $3,000

Your split: 100%

Tradeify Growth funded

Qualifying days: 5 days of $150+

Other conditions: balance of $53,000; 35% consistency

Amount per request: $500 minimum; first cap $1,500

Your split: 90%

MFFU Flex sim funded

Qualifying days: 5 winning days of $150+

Other conditions: $500 net profit since the last payout

Amount per request: 50% of profits, cap $2,000; $500 minimum

Your split: 80%

Two ideas repeat. First, a qualifying day is a day that closed with at least a set profit. Losing days don't reset the count at most firms, but they do lower your balance, and some plans also need a minimum total. MFFU gives the example of five $150 winning days plus one −$1,000 day: the day count is met, but total profit is −$250, so there is no payout. Second, the count usually restarts after each payout. Tradeify says the day count "resets to zero after each successful payout".

The buffer: what a payout does to your floor

A buffer is the distance between your balance and the loss floor. It is the only thing that keeps a funded account open on a bad day.

Several firms raise the floor at the first payout:

  • Topstep: "After your first Payout: Your MLL is set to $0 regardless of where it was before. The remaining balance becomes your effective loss floor."
  • MFFU Flex: after the first payout the maximum loss limit "moves to $100" and "becomes fixed permanently".
  • Apex: the safety net, "your account's drawdown limit plus $100", stays for the life of the account, and "only profit above the safety net is eligible" to be paid.

So the same profit gives different results. Here is one hypothetical $3,000 profit, taking the largest first payout each plan allows:

PlanFirst payoutYou receiveBalance afterFloor afterRoom left
Topstep XFA$1,500$1,350$1,500$0$1,500
MFFU Flex$1,500$1,200$1,500$100$1,400
Apex EOD PA$900$900$2,100 profit$2,100 profit$0

On Apex, the safety net is $2,100 above the start, so of the $3,000 profit only $900 is payable, and taking all of it leaves the balance exactly at the net. That shows the trade-off clearly: every dollar you take out is a dollar that can't absorb the next loss.

A worked path through one payout

Hypothetical. A trader on a $50K XFA makes steady profits for ten days, takes a first payout, then keeps trading:

On day 7 the balance first closed at $2,000 or more, so the floor locked at $0 ("Once your balance reaches $2,000, the MLL locks at $0 permanently"). By day 10 the balance is $2,000 with 8 days of $150 or more, so the Standard path is met. The trader asks for 50%: $1,000, of which 90% ($900) is theirs. The floor stays at $0, but the balance above it halves: the $1,000 left is now the whole buffer. The smallest buffer after that was $950, on the −$400 day. Without the payout it would have been $1,950. At $950, three more days like that would close the account.

That is why many funded traders cut size after a payout until the buffer is rebuilt. PF-06's idea of sizing from the room you have applies even more here.

Choosing how much to take

There is no single right answer, but you can make it a rule instead of a mood. Three common approaches:

Take the maximum

How it works: Request the most allowed each time.

Trade-off: Money out sooner; thinnest buffer; most likely to lose the account on a bad week.

Fixed buffer first

How it works: Only request profit above a buffer you choose, e.g. one full loss limit.

Trade-off: Slower first payout; much more room afterwards.

Split the difference

How it works: Take half of what is allowed, keep the rest.

Trade-off: Balances cash now against room later.

Whichever you choose, write it down with a number. Also remember the timing rules: Tradeify says funds are paid "within 24–48 hours" after approval, and that a request "cannot be edited or canceled". If you fall below the threshold before approval, "your payout will be denied".

A payout-day checklist

Before you press the request button, run through this list. It takes two minutes and catches most of the avoidable denials:

  1. Count your qualifying days on the firm's dashboard, not in your head. Check the minimum profit per day for your account size.
  2. Check the balance or net-profit condition against the published number, after fees and commissions.
  3. Check any consistency rule. Divide your best day by total profit since the last payout. If it is too high, keep trading normal days until it drops.
  4. Decide the amount using your written payout rule, and work out the floor and buffer afterwards.
  5. Stop or cut size until it is approved. A loss that drops you below the threshold before approval can cost you the payout.
  6. Record it: date, amount requested, amount received, and the balance and floor afterwards.

Keep the list next to your risk plan from PF-06. Over several payout cycles, your records will show whether your payout rule is leaving enough room.

Payout caps and the road to live

Many funded accounts don't last forever by design. Apex allows a "maximum of six payouts" per Performance Account, rising from $1,500 to $3,000 on a 50K, and then "the PA is closed". The six 50K caps add up to $13,000 before split. MFFU Flex lists a maximum of 5 sim payouts, and a move to a live account after "five consecutive approved payouts", a $100,000 sim payout cap, or a risk-team review.

Live accounts are different again. MFFU's live Flex account starts with "an initial balance of $2,000". Topstep says the move to its Live Funded Account "isn't automatic", is reviewed "case by case", and starts at 20% of your cumulative XFA balance, with the rest held in reserve (PF-01 worked through an example). Topstep can also move a live trader back to a simulated account, which it calls a "Shoulder Tap", and says "there is no warning". So plan for the funded stage as a series of accounts, not one account that grows forever.

Taxes and paperwork

Payouts are income paid to you by a company, usually as a contractor. How they are taxed depends on where you live, so we won't give tax advice. Keep a record of every payout, every fee and every reset, with dates, and ask a qualified tax professional in your country how to report them.

Common mistakes

Reading payout rules only after passing

Better approach: Read them before you buy the evaluation, as part of PF-03's vetting.

Keeping evaluation size after the floor moves up

Better approach: Size from the buffer you actually have; cut size after a payout.

Counting losing days as progress

Better approach: Only qualifying days count, and some plans also need a minimum net profit.

Trading big right after requesting

Better approach: Falling below the threshold before approval can void the payout.

Assuming an account lasts forever

Better approach: Check payout caps and the account's end conditions.

Practice exercises

  1. For your plan, list the qualifying-day rule, minimum balance or profit, consistency rule, minimum and maximum payout, split and payout cap.
  2. Take a $3,000 profit and work out your first payout, what you receive, the floor afterwards and the room left.
  3. Write your payout rule: how much you take, and the minimum buffer you always leave.
  4. Write your size rule for the first week after a payout.

Self-check quiz

1. What happens to Topstep's Maximum Loss Limit after the first XFA payout?

It is set to $0, so the balance left becomes your loss floor buffer.

2. On Apex's 50K EOD PA, which profit can be paid out?

Only profit above the $52,100 safety net, with a $500 minimum request.

3. Five $150 winning days and one −$1,000 day on MFFU Flex: eligible?

No. Net profit is −$250, below the $500 required.

4. Why cut size after a payout?

The buffer is smaller, so the same loss is a bigger share of the room you have.

5. Is the move to a live account automatic at Topstep?

No. It is reviewed case by case.
